Case report
Patient: 58-year-old man.
Chief complaint: Rigidity of the head/neck and lower limbs.
Past history: At age 56 he received an intramuscular tetanus toxoid injection for a right finger/hand injury.
Family history: Nothing of note.
Smoking: 40-50 cigarettes/day for 32 years.
Present illness: On April 6, 1998, tightness of the left half of the face, difficulty moving the tongue, difficulty speaking, and difficulty swallowing appeared and gradually worsened. Around April 22, involuntary rapid movements appeared on the face triggered by tactile or painful stimuli. From early May, stiffness of the lower limbs appeared, along with reflex myoclonus in which the head quickly retracted (extended backward) when he was touched. These symptoms worsened further, and he became unable to stand or walk; he was admitted to our hospital on June 15.

On admission, general physical examination showed no abnormality. Neurological findings: the left facial expression muscles were rigid, the forehead wrinkles disappeared and were tonically contracted. The bilateral pterygoid and sternocleidomastoid muscles were rigid, and he held a posture with the shoulders hunched/squared. Tongue movement was poor in all directions, and the tongue tip could not pass the lips. Rigidity of the trunk and upper limbs was not evident. The lower limbs were mildly rigid with left-side predominance, worsened by active and passive movement, becoming board-like; these also disappeared during sleep. Somatosensory or acoustic stimulation of the face and occiput elicited myoclonus in which the neck retracted and both shoulders elevated; no movement propagating to the upper or lower limbs was seen. This head/neck myoclonus was not provoked by tapping of the trunk, upper limbs, or lower limbs. Somatosensory stimulation of the lower limbs elicited myoclonus that rapidly stiffened the entire bilateral lower limbs; this movement was localized to both lower limbs and was not provoked by tapping of the head/neck, trunk, or upper limbs. Both the head/neck and bilateral lower-limb myoclonus tended to weaken with repeated stimulation. Upper-limb tendon reflexes were normal; other regions could not be evaluated because myoclonus appeared. No pathological reflexes were found. On standing he assumed a forward-leaning posture and fell because of lower-limb rigidity, and walking was impossible.

Blood biochemistry showed Hb 12.6 g/dL and ESR 10 mm/h (mild changes). Antinuclear antibody was speckled at 160x; all others were below 20x. Tetanus antibody showed a very slight elevation at 0.31 IU/mL. Anti-GAD antibody and anti-amphiphysin antibody (assayed by De Camilli et al.) were both negative. Anti-cardiolipin, anti-skeletal muscle, anti-thyroid, anti-thyroglobulin, anti-pancreatic islet, anti-Scl-70, anti-RNP, anti-Sm, anti-SS-A, anti-SS-B, anti-ss-DNA, anti-ds-DNA, thyroglobulin, and microsomal antibodies were all negative. The tumor marker NCC-ST-439 was elevated at 28.6 U/mL, while NSE, SCC, CA19-9, CEA, PA, and PAP were all negative. CSF findings were normal: cell count 1/mm3 (mononuclear:polymorphonuclear = 1:0), protein 33 mg/dL; as in serum, anti-GAD and anti-amphiphysin antibodies were negative. MRI of the head, neck, chest, and lumbar regions showed no abnormality. The H reflex in the soleus had an H/M ratio of 10% or less, and recurrent (Renshaw cell) inhibition could not be evaluated. Lower-limb somatosensory evoked potentials showed no latency abnormality and no giant SEP. Needle EMG showed only normal motor units. Nerve conduction velocity and EEG showed no abnormality.

When surface EMG of the bilateral splenius capitis muscles was recorded during electrical stimulation of the nasal tip, the fastest latency after stimulation showed bilaterally synchronous contraction at 15 ms, with synchronous contraction also at 50 ms (Fig 1). Electrical stimulation of the left dorsal foot skin elicited stiffening movements localized to both lower limbs. Surface EMG of the left quadriceps femoris, hamstrings, tibialis anterior, and gastrocnemius showed a reproducible pattern of myoclonus and continuous muscle discharge: the fastest latency was 41 ms, followed by 5-6 nearly synchronous repetitive muscle contractions at intervals of 59-84 ms, and from around 250 ms continuous discharge appeared in all muscles and continued for several seconds while decaying. The first contraction was most distinct in the tibialis anterior near the stimulation site, showing a characteristic waveform that grew larger and spread to nearby muscles through the third repetition (Fig 2). The latencies of myoclonus in each muscle (ms) were as follows -- quadriceps femoris: 122 (2nd), 188 (3rd), 254 (4th); hamstrings: 121 (2nd), 183 (3rd), 251 (4th), 326 (5th); tibialis anterior: 41 (1st), 125 (2nd), 191 (3rd), 255 (4th), 327 (5th); gastrocnemius: 49 (1st), 123 (2nd), 182 (3rd), 256 (4th), 328 (5th).

Gallium scintigraphy showed accumulation in the mediastinum, and contrast-enhanced chest CT showed a paraaortic tumor mass of approximately 4 x 2 x 2 cm with mild swelling of bilateral hilar lymph nodes (Fig 3). Thyroid, breast, and cardiac ultrasonography, abdominal CT, upper gastrointestinal endoscopy, barium enema, bronchoscopy, and bone scintigraphy showed no abnormality.

With oral diazepam 20 mg, symptoms improved markedly: the myoclonus localized to the lower limbs disappeared, and only mild rigidity of the left face and tongue and reflex myoclonus localized to the head/neck on facial/occipital skin stimulation remained. After tumor resection accompanying an open-chest tumor biopsy performed on August 11, these symptoms improved further and only very slightly remained (Fig 4). Pathological diagnosis of the biopsy tissue showed only a small amount of undifferentiated carcinoma with mucin production, considered to be metastatic to mediastinal lymph nodes; the primary tissue could not be identified. Postoperative NCC-ST-439 decreased to 8.0 U/mL, and repeat gallium scintigraphy showed no abnormal accumulation. To date no clear primary lesion has been identified, and there has been no worsening of symptoms.

Discussion

This case was diagnosed as stiff-man syndrome based on adult onset, chronic progression, persistent muscle rigidity, persistent muscle discharge on surface EMG, disappearance of rigidity during sleep, marked efficacy of diazepam, and normal CSF findings. Because the anti-tetanus antibody was very slightly elevated, chronic tetanus was considered in the differential diagnosis, but it was thought unlikely because there was no history of trauma immediately before onset, the symptoms were left-right asymmetric, and typical findings such as trismus were absent; the antibody elevation was attributed to prior tetanus toxoid use.

In 1980, Leigh et al. reported a case of stiff-man syndrome with prominent reflex myoclonus, naming it "jerking stiff-man syndrome," and Alberca et al. made a similar report. Subsequently, Meinck et al., based on clinical and electrophysiological study of 8 cases, reported that reflex myoclonus is rather frequently observed in stiff-man syndrome. Meinck et al. in particular observed 1-3 synchronous fast contractions on surface EMG with synchronous-contraction intervals of 60-80 ms, followed at the end of the synchronous contractions by a decaying continuous discharge; they noted that this reflex myoclonus is not seen in other myoclonic disorders such as reticular reflex myoclonus, Lance-Adams syndrome, Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, or psychogenic generalized reflex jerks, positioned it as a characteristic finding of the disease, and named it "spasmodic reflex myoclonus." They further stated that the order of muscle recruitment in this spasmodic reflex myoclonus follows the spinal cord and may run along the propriospinal tract, suggesting that it is also important when considering the etiology of muscle rigidity in stiff-man syndrome. The myoclonus elicited by dorsal foot stimulation in our case closely resembled the involuntary movement reported by Meinck et al. -- 1-3 synchronous fast contractions, synchronous-contraction intervals of 60-80 ms, and a decaying continuous discharge at the end -- and was similar to what they called spasmodic reflex myoclonus, an involuntary movement suspected to arise by this mechanism. However, the myoclonus elicited by dorsal foot stimulation in our case was localized to lower-limb muscles and was nearly synchronous, so from its latency differences we could not prove whether it was a phenomenon mediated by the propriospinal tract. Because the fastest myoclonus latency on dorsal foot stimulation was 41 ms, comparable to the Achilles tendon reflex, an excitability abnormality at the lumbar spinal cord level was considered possible.

The reflex myoclonus on head stimulation, in which the neck retracted, resembled a so-called startle response. On surface EMG of the splenius capitis during nasal-tip stimulation, the fastest contraction latency was 15 ms, only slightly slower than the R1 latency of the blink reflex; considering also the latency difference between the orbicularis oculi and splenius capitis, the origin of the myoclonus was considered to be the brainstem. Although reflex myoclonus complicating stiff-man syndrome is not rare, in our case the head/neck and lower-limb reflex myoclonus differed in their response to treatment, and although the detailed pathophysiology is unclear, their origins may also differ electrophysiologically.

Among tumors complicating stiff-man syndrome as a paraneoplastic syndrome, breast cancer is most common; others include small cell lung cancer, Hodgkin disease, colon cancer, and thymoma. Anti-GAD antibody, which is positive in about 60% of stiff-man syndrome, has not been reported positive in paraneoplastic stiff-man syndrome, so some immune-mediated pathology associated with malignancy is postulated. Folli and De Camilli reported cases of stiff-man syndrome associated with breast cancer that were positive for anti-amphiphysin antibody. Rosin et al. reported a breast-cancer case that was anti-GAD-negative and anti-amphiphysin-positive in which symptoms improved after tumor resection, and, including the two earlier cases, suggested the existence of a paraneoplastic syndrome presenting stiff-man syndrome, breast cancer, and anti-amphiphysin antibody positivity. In our case, antibodies against both GAD and amphiphysin were negative. However, because symptoms improved further after resection of the mediastinal tumor, the possibility was suggested that the condition involves a paraneoplastic syndrome caused by some immune abnormality other than GAD or amphiphysin.
